conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll move at whatever pace feels comfortable. I’ll ask 10 questions about the past seven days, and we’ll talk through each one together. Ready to begin?

1. Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy things or look forward to outings the way you normally would?
Yeah, I’ve still been looking forward to seeing friends or going for walks with the baby. It’s not quite the same—everything takes more planning now—but I do still enjoy getting out.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Oh, definitely. My husband and I still joke around, especially when the baby makes those silly milk-drunk faces. I laugh pretty easily—maybe not quite as often just because I’m tired, but the sense of humor is still there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I still get excited about little things—like our weekly coffee meet-up with the moms’ group or even just a quiet evening once the baby’s down. I look forward to them, maybe just a bit less energy to enjoy them fully, but the excitement’s still there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I don’t really beat myself up. If the baby’s extra fussy or I’m running late, I figure it’s just part of the learning curve—I might think “I could have timed that better,” but I don’t sit around feeling guilty or blaming myself.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Not for no good reason—mostly just the usual new-mom worries, like checking if she’s breathing when she’s asleep. Once I peek in the crib and see her chest moving, I’m fine. It’s not constant or out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that panicky feeling. I get startled when she cries suddenly, but it passes right away—I wouldn’t call it scared or panicky without a reason.
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes, yeah—like when she cluster-feeds and I can’t even get a shower in. It feels a bit much for a moment, but once she settles I can breathe again. It’s not every day, just every now and then.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been okay. I crash pretty hard once she’s down for the night—my husband gives her a bottle so I can get a solid stretch. I haven’t felt so upset that it kept me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt really sad or miserable—maybe a little wistful for how simple errands used to be, but it passes quickly. Overall I still feel pretty steady.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I think I teared up once last week when I couldn’t get her to latch after multiple tries, but it was just for a minute and I was more frustrated than anything. Nothing that felt like real crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that, overall, you're adapting well to new motherhood. You still laugh with your husband, look forward to your moms' group coffee dates, and generally view the day-to-day challenges as part of the normal learning curve. While you occasionally feel a bit overwhelmed during cluster-feeding or briefly wistful for pre-baby simplicity, these moments pass quickly and haven't clouded your ability to enjoy life or care for yourself and your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 6, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes occasional overwhelm during cluster-feeding but regains composure, matching "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 6 places you in the "depression not likely" range (< 9). You endorsed only mild, situation-specific stress (<sym>things getting on top of me</sym> scored 2) and minimal reduction in laughter/anticipation (each 1). All core mood items (<sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance from unhappiness</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, and <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym>) were denied or scored 0. These findings fall well below <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which require ≥ 5 symptoms (including either depressed mood or loss of interest) for at least two weeks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue attending your moms' group for social support
2. Build brief self-care moments into cluster-feeding times (water, snack, audiobook) to ease <sym>overwhelm</sym>
3. Re-screen with EPDS at the 6-week postpartum visit or sooner if mood changes
4. Maintain current bedtime routine and partner bottle shift to protect sleep
5. Keep pediatric or PCP follow-up appointments; mention any future mood, anxiety, or self-harm concerns promptly
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Absence of persistent low mood, anhedonia, pathological guilt, or crying spells
- Occasional situational “wistfulness” and transient frustration with feeding; no mood-related insomnia or hopelessness
- Normal-range anticipatory anxiety (baby’s safety, latch issues); no spontaneous panic or pervasive worry
- Intermittent feeling “a bit much” when cluster-feeding; rebounds quickly—no global sense of being overwhelmed
- Denies any self-harm ideation

Pattern summary:
Overall affective stability; maintains capacity for pleasure, humor, and social connection. Brief, context-appropriate stress reactions only.

Screening significance:
Current responses do not indicate elevated risk for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder. No safety concerns identified at this time.
